h1:
Southern Thai Food in Phang Nga
Gaeng Tai Pla, Kua Kling, Stink Beans & Yellow Curry
intro: Phang Nga is one of those provinces where southern Thai food is still the real deal — fresh-pounded curry paste, deep-yellow turmeric, fragrant shrimp paste, and heat that actually bites. The kind people in the south eat every day. Several restaurants here have made the Michelin Guide, and we’ve pulled together spots that locals go back to, backed by real reviews — from rich, funky gaeng tai pla to dry-fried kua kling scented with kaffir lime leaves.

blocks.html: Southern Thai food in Phang Nga is the genuine article. Local restaurants still pound their own curry paste, load in the turmeric, and don’t pull back on the heat. If you love bold flavors, you’re in the right place. If chili isn’t your strong suit, just tell the kitchen you’d like it mild — because the southern Thai baseline for ‘medium spice’ can be a shock if you’re used to central Thai food. Most restaurants in Phang Nga are spread across different districts: Mueang Phang Nga, Takua Pa, Takua Thung, Thai Mueang, and Khao Lak. Worth planning your route before you head out.

blocks.text: 4 Southern Dishes You Have to Try

items.name: Gaeng Tai Pla
items.blurb: A punchy curry built on fermented fish entrails — salty, fiery, and layered with fresh-pounded spices. Loaded with fingerroot, then padded out with whatever’s in season: pumpkin, eggplant, long beans, bamboo shoots, sometimes shredded grilled fish. It’s the dish that tells you whether a southern kitchen is the real deal. Eat it with steamed rice and fresh raw vegetables on the side.

items.name: Kua Kling
items.blurb: Minced meat — pork, chicken, or beef — dry-fried with southern curry paste until fragrant and almost no liquid remains. Finished with sliced kaffir lime leaves. It hits hard with heat and no broth to soften the blow. The classic pairing: steamed rice and cucumber slices to cool things down. For people who like serious spice, this tends to be the one they can’t stop ordering.

items.name: Pad Sataw (Stink Beans with Shrimp Paste)
items.blurb: Fresh sataw beans stir-fried with shrimp paste and whole prawns. The smell is strong and distinctive — if you’re a fan, you’ll be hooked immediately. The flavor is salty-savory with a touch of sweetness and just enough heat. Works beautifully over rice and never gets old. Some places swap the prawns for pork belly, which is equally good.

items.name: Gaeng Luang (Yellow Curry)
items.blurb: Southern-style sour curry colored deep gold from fresh turmeric. Sharp, tangy, and spicy — common additions include sea bass, pickled bamboo shoots, or young coconut shoots. The broth has a lip-tingling acidity that makes you want to keep spooning it up. A staple at any proper southern table.

blocks.title: Order Like a Local
blocks.html: Always get phak nao (a plate of fresh raw vegetables — cucumber, long beans, ivy gourd leaves) alongside gaeng tai pla or kua kling. The raw veg cuts through the heat and lets you keep eating longer. Most southern restaurants throw it in for free without you having to ask.

blocks.text: 10 Southern Thai Restaurants in Phang Nga That Locals Go To

blocks.html: These are places that are currently open, have consistent real reviews behind them, and several have Michelin Guide recognition. Prices are approximate ranges — always worth double-checking ahead of time since seafood costs shift with the season. Many of these spots have a weekly closing day, so a quick call before making a long drive is genuinely worthwhile.

items.name: Krua Luang Then
items.blurb: A southern Thai restaurant in Takua Pa district that earned a spot in the Michelin Guide. Genuinely authentic flavors — standouts are the kua moo (dry-fried pork curry), gaeng tai pla with catfish and cha-phluu leaves, and spicy stir-fried duck. The curry paste is pounded fresh, and the fragrance shows it. A go-to for Michelin hunters visiting Phang Nga. Open for lunch and dinner in set sittings.
items.meta: Takua Pa District · Open 11:00–13:00 and 17:00–20:00 · Michelin Guide

items.name: Ran Nai Mueang (Takua Pa)
items.blurb: Another Michelin Guide pick in Takua Pa, known for their yam nai mueang — a sharp salad tossed with prawns, squid, and local herbs. Beyond that, the menu covers curries and southern stir-fries done properly. Bold enough to satisfy serious spice lovers. Closed Wednesdays — call ahead to confirm hours.
items.meta: Takua Pa District · Open 11:00–14:00 and 16:00–21:00 (closed Wed) · Michelin Guide

items.name: Ran Roedang (Lam Kaen)
items.blurb: A well-known southern Thai and seafood restaurant in Lam Kaen, Thai Mueang district — with a Michelin Guide listing. Stars of the menu include moo kua glua (salt-stir-fried pork), squid simmered in black sauce, crab curry with cha-phluu leaves, and cha chu. Strong southern flavors and a riverside setting. Book ahead on weekends.
items.meta: Opposite Lam Kaen SAO, Thai Mueang District · Open 10:30–15:00 and 18:00–20:30 (closed Wed) · Michelin Guide

items.name: Ran Duang (Mueang Phang Nga)
items.blurb: A southern Thai restaurant in Phang Nga town where locals meet up for a proper meal. Highlights include crispy salted fish, sour soup with pork knuckle, squid in black sauce, and a solid spread of southern dishes. Conveniently located in town — ideal if you’re staying in the centre and want real southern food without a long drive.
items.meta: Mueang Phang Nga · Local prices THB 80–250/dish

items.name: Krua Ton Fon (Thap Put)
items.blurb: A budget-friendly southern Thai spot in Thap Put district with a Michelin Guide nod. Dry-fried pork, crab curry, and young coconut shoot with coconut milk are the ones to order. Homestyle flavors, full seasoning, open through the day — a good stop if you’re passing through Thap Put on the way somewhere else.
items.meta: Thap Put District · Open 07:00–21:00 · Michelin Guide, budget-friendly

items.name: Krua Bai Toei (Takua Pa)
items.blurb: A long-running spot in Takua Pa that locals have been going to for years. Salt-stir-fried pork, fish-head soup, and green mango nam prik are the things people keep coming back for. Rustic southern home cooking, unapologetically bold. Good if you want flavors that haven’t been adjusted for outside tastes.

items.name: Khanom Jeen Pa Son (Mueang Phang Nga)
items.blurb: A self-service rice noodle shop near the Chinese shrine on Bua Ra Ya Road in Phang Nga town. Ladles out several sauces including gaeng tai pla and southern coconut curry — you choose your own portions. Fresh raw vegetables included at no charge. Michelin Guide listed. Best for breakfast or lunch; closes in the afternoon.
items.meta: Sanjao Sai Area, Bua Ra Ya Rd, Mueang Phang Nga · Open 10:00–17:00 (closed Mon–Tue) · Michelin Guide

items.name: Ran Nai Mueang Khao Lak
items.blurb: A southern Thai option in the Khao Lak area for people staying beachside who don’t want to drive into town. Coconut curry with Thai eggplant, three-flavour vegetable stir-fry, and shrimp paste stir-fry are the picks. The cooking is tuned slightly milder while still reading as southern. Handy and close to beach accommodation.
items.meta: Khao Lak, Takua Pa District · Slightly higher prices than in-town restaurants

items.name: Ran Yim Yim (Bang Muang, Takua Pa)
items.blurb: A no-frills neighbourhood southern Thai spot in Bang Muang, Takua Pa. Known for stuffed tofu, salted pork, and fried fish southern-style. Unpretentious home-kitchen flavors — the kind of place where Takua Pa people eat on a regular weekday, not somewhere dressed up for visitors.
items.meta: Bang Muang, Takua Pa District · Local prices

items.name: Khao Kaeng Southern Curry Shop (Mueang Phang Nga)
items.blurb: A rice-and-curry counter in Phang Nga town with several southern pots to choose from — gaeng tai pla, kua kling, spicy stir-fries, and yellow curry. Pick your curry, get it ladled over rice, done. Cheap, quick, and filling. Good for a solo meal or when you’re in a hurry. Go early and the selection will be at its fullest.
items.meta: Mueang Phang Nga · Rice plate THB 45–70

blocks.title: Honest Heads-Up
blocks.html: Authentic southern Thai food is more intensely seasoned than most visitors expect — heat, salt, and sour all hitting at once. If your spice tolerance is low, start with something more approachable like pad sataw or young coconut shoot with coconut milk, then work up to gaeng tai pla or kua kling. · Most of the Michelin spots are spread across separate districts (Takua Pa, Thai Mueang, Thap Put) — you’ll need a car and a route plan. Many also have a fixed weekly closing day, so call ahead before making a long drive.

blocks.text: How to Get the Most Out of Eating Southern Thai

items: Start in the middle — open with pad sataw or coconut shoot curry before jumping to gaeng tai pla or kua kling, which hit harder
Ask for extra phak nao — the plate of raw vegetables cuts through the heat and extends how long you can eat; it’s almost always free
Eat it with steamed rice — southern Thai curries are built to go with rice, not eaten on their own
Check days and sittings — several Michelin spots close Wednesdays or open only during specific service windows; a quick call saves a wasted trip
Say your spice level — asking for mild is fine, kitchens are used to adjusting, no need to feel awkward about it

faq.q: Which restaurants in Phang Nga serve the most authentic southern Thai flavors?
faq.a: For full-strength, uncompromised southern Thai cooking, Krua Luang Then and Ran Nai Mueang in Takua Pa district are the top picks — both are Michelin Guide listed and known for cooking that doesn’t dial anything back. In Phang Nga town itself, Ran Duang and Khanom Jeen Pa Son are solid options that don’t require a long drive.

faq.q: What is gaeng tai pla and how spicy is it?
faq.a: Gaeng tai pla is a curry made from fermented fish entrails, fingerroot, and seasonal vegetables — the flavor is predominantly salty with serious heat. By central Thai standards it’s genuinely spicy. If chili isn’t your thing, ask for mild when you order, and eat it with a side of fresh raw vegetables and plenty of steamed rice to balance it out.

faq.q: Which restaurants in Phang Nga have Michelin Guide recognition?
faq.a: Several spots in Phang Nga have made the Michelin Guide, including Krua Luang Then, Ran Nai Mueang, Ran Roedang, Krua Ton Fon, and Khanom Jeen Pa Son. They’re spread across Takua Pa, Thai Mueang, Thap Put, and Mueang Phang Nga — check opening hours and weekly closing days before you go.

faq.q: Do I need a car to eat southern Thai food in Phang Nga?
faq.a: For spots in Phang Nga town — Ran Duang, Khanom Jeen Pa Son, and the local curry counters — you can manage on foot or with a short ride. But the well-known Michelin restaurants like Krua Luang Then, Ran Nai Mueang, and Ran Roedang are in different districts and require a car or a planned taxi trip.

faq.q: Stink beans have a strong smell — is it worth trying them if I’ve never had them before?
faq.a: The smell is real and distinct — first-timers sometimes find it off-putting before they taste it. But pad sataw with shrimp paste and prawns is actually one of the more approachable southern Thai dishes: salty, savory, mildly sweet, moderate heat. Start with a small order. Many people who were skeptical end up ordering it again. It’s an easier entry point than gaeng tai pla.
